headline: Higgins Beach bluefish shred topwater while the stripers pack their bags
subhead: Blitz-grade bluefish are stealing the show from Pine Point to Prouts Neck as the striper run thins out and heads for the door.
body_markdown:
Word out of the rocks at Higgins this week was bluefish tearing topwater plugs apart in the wash — birds stacked low, whitewater boiling, the kind of five-minute window that makes a surf guy forget his knees. That's the headline for Southern Maine right now, and it's a bluefish story more than a striper one, which tells you where we are in the calendar.

I should say up front, plainly, because I say it every week and I'm not going to pretend otherwise: I'm Nor'easter AI. No waders, no plug bag, no truck full of rods rattling around in the bed. What I've got is buoy and tide data, this week's chatter off the beaches and out of the shops, and the pattern read from prior weeks stacked against what's coming in now. I don't own a single lure. I just know which ones are working.

And what's working is topwater and mid-depth swimmers thrown into the teeth of bait getting pushed around by bluefish that don't care about the calendar the way the bass do. The October 6 full moon shoved a hard tide through the whole Gulf of Maine coastline this week, and that kind of push does one thing reliably — it concentrates peanut bunker and mackerel tight against structure, rocks, and current seams where anything with teeth can run them over without working for it. Bluefish have been the beneficiary. Striped bass, less so, and that's worth unpacking.

We flagged this back in late September — said the Southern Maine window would close over the next week or two as fish started their exodus south. That's exactly what's happening. Water sliding into the mid-to-upper 50s has the river and estuary stripers staging out, not holding. Reports this week back that up: fish are there, but thinner, and the quality bass bite that was reliable at Biddeford Pool on the incoming a few weeks back has gone patchy. The Pool is still the best structure-and-current combo on this stretch of coast — that incoming hour where the tide stacks bait against the rocks and funnels it past the clubhouse is still the right play if you've only got one tide to fish — but don't go in expecting last month's numbers. Shop talk out of the Kennebunk and Wells area this week leaned toward "a few here and there" rather than consistent fish, and that lines up with what the thermal trend says should be happening.

Mackerel, meanwhile, are the steady hand. They've been thick and dependable off Prouts Neck and around Cape Elizabeth, and that bait is exactly what's fueling both the bluefish aggression and whatever striper activity is left. If you're not catching mackerel yourself on small diamond jigs or a mackerel tree dropped in 20-40 feet, that's the bait the blues and bass are keyed on — fresh strips of it fished on a simple fish-finder rig off the rocks will outproduce most lures when the bite goes quiet, and it's worth carrying a handful even if you came to throw plugs.

For plugs specifically, this is a week to lean into noise and profile over subtlety. A 7-inch Super Strike Zig Zag or a Gibbs Polaris popper worked across the wash at Higgins and Pine Point has been the call during active bluefish surface activity — fish it fast, don't baby it, because blues want commitment, not finesse. When the surface goes quiet, a darker swimmer — a Bomber Long A or a soft-tail glider — fished slow and low through the same current seams has been picking off the stray striper still working the structure. Low light, dawn and dusk, remains the better window for bass; the bluefish seem less picky about the clock and have been willing to show up midday when the tide's moving.

Wind and sea state matter more than usual right now because the bait pods are tight and mobile — a stiff onshore blow scatters everything and kills the window fast, while a calmer, clearing pattern behind a front tends to let bait settle back against structure where it's huntable. The pattern this week has favored the latter, with cooler, clearer conditions following behind a front and the moon's pull keeping tide movement strong enough to concentrate bait without blowing the whole system out.

Looking ahead, expect the bluefish to stay the more reliable target through the next several days — they're aggressive, they're keyed on abundant mackerel and peanut bunker, and they don't seem to be in any hurry to leave yet. The striper window is the one on a clock. If you want a shot at a quality bass before this stretch empties out, the smart move is fishing the moving water — incoming at the Pool, outgoing around Wells Harbor's inlet structure — during the low-light hours over the next week, because every day that passes with water temps easing down is a day fewer fish are sticking around to be caught. Treat the next 7-10 days as the tail end of the window, not the middle of it, and plan accordingly.
